texts.preamble: Samima Khatoon vs Mohd. Iqbal Nasir on 9 September, 2025 In The Court Of Sh. Anubhav Sharma, Civil Judge-01 (South West) Dwarka Court, New Delhi Unique case Id No:104 Cnr No. Dlsw030001432020 In The Matter Of: - Smt. Samima Khatoon W/O Late Mohd.Noorul Nabi R/O H.No.129A, R-Extension, Mohan Garden, Uttam Nagar, New Delhi-110059 Versus Mohd.Iqbal Nasir S/O Late Mohd.Noorul Nabi R/O H.No.129A, R-Extension, Mohan Garden, Uttam Nagar, New Delhi-110059 . Date of Institution : 23.01. Date of framing of issues : 10.12. Date of final arguments : 08.08. Date of Decision : 09.09. Decision : Dismis Suit For Permanent And Mandatory Injunction Judgment. 1.
texts.facts: By this judgment this Court shall dispose of a suit for permanent and mandatory injunction filed by the Plaintiff against the Defendant. 2. It is pertinent to mention that the plaintiff initially filed the present suit against two defendants. However, during the course of the proceedings, an application for amendment was filed, which was allowed Digitally signed by ANUBHAV ANUBHAV SHARMA Date: Pursuant to the said order, the amended plaint was taken on record. As per the amended plaint, the name of Defendant No.2, Smt. Darksha Sheikh, wife of Mohd. Iqbal Nasir (Defendant No.1), has been struck off from the array of parties in the present case." AVERMENTS OF THE PLAINT: - 3. Succinctly, it is the case of the Plaintiff that She is the absolute owner and in possession of property bearing No. 129A, R- Extension, Mohan Garden, Uttam Nagar, New Delhi-110059 ( herein after referred as to "suit property"), measuring 50 square yards and comprising a ground floor with two rooms, kitchen, latrine, and bathroom, and a first floor with one room. The plaintiff allowed her son --the defendant--to reside in the suit property as a licensee out of love and affection. The defendant is married to Smt. Darksha Sheikh and has two children from the said marriage. 4. Further mentioned that however, shortly after the marriage, the defendant and his wife started misbehaving with the plaintiff, using abusive language, assaulting her, and denying her basic necessities like food and medicine. Due to continued harassment and threats to her life, including attempts to involve anti-social elements to forcibly retain the property, the plaintiff, by way of a public notice dated 12.06.2019 published in the newspaper "Virat Vaibhav", debarred the defendant and his family from all her movable and immovable properties and revoked the license granted to him. 5. It is further averred that despite repeated verbal and written requests, including a legal notice dated 28.08.2019 sent via Speed Post, the defendant refused to vacate the premises and instead threatened the plaintiff with dire consequences. The defendant has also attempted to sell or create third-party interest in the suit property using false and fabricated documents, which came to the plaintiff's knowledge through reliable Civil Suit No.104/20 Judgment dt.09.09.2025 Page no. 2 of 21 sources. 6. Furthermore, on multiple occasions, the plaintiff approached the local police at PS Ranhola to file complaints against the defendant's acts of abuse, harassment, and threats, but no legal action was taken, and she was advised to approach the court. Consequently, due to fear for her safety, the plaintiff was forced to leave her own house and has been living with her daughter since 25.02.2022. 7. The Plaintiff further submits that she continues to be the lawful and rightful owner of the suit property and maintains constructive possession thereof, as her personal belongings, valuables, and household effects remain within the premises. The Defendant, who was initially permitted to occupy the suit property as a licensee, is now wrongfully and unlawfully retaining possession, having no legal right, title, or interest therein. It is further submitted that the Defendant has become an unauthorized occupant and is willfully obstructing the Plaintiff's ingress into the suit property, thereby unlawfully depriving her of access and enjoyment of her own premises. 8. The plaintiff claims 8,000/- per month as license fee from 12.06.2019 till the date of actual possession is handed back, excluding Samima Khatoon vs Mohd. Iqbal Nasir on 9 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/172214367/ 2 water and electricity charges, and also seeks 500/- per day as damages for unlawful occupation. Due to the continued illegal possession and threats, the plaintiff has suffered immense mental agony and harassment. change/demolish the real structure of the suit property i.e property bearing 129-A, Extension, Mohan Garden, Uttam Nagar, New Delhi-110059, which is better shown in Red Colour in the attached Site Plan and defendant be directed to vacate and handover peaceful possession of the suit property. ii. Cost of the suit may also be awarded in favor of the Plaintiff and against the Defendant. AVERMENTS OF WRITTEN STATEMENT: - 9. It is liable to be rejected under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, on the grounds of improper valuation for the purposes of court fees and jurisdiction. After the amendment of the plaint in the present suit, the previously framed issues were revisited, and the following issues were framed by the Learned Predecessor of this Court through vide order dated on 22.09.2023: vi. Photocopy of the ownership documents of suit property i.e. GPA, agreement to sale deed, affidavit, receipt, possession letter and Will are collectively Ex.PW1/5(colly). (OSR). vii. Copy of electricity bills are collectively marked as mark X (Ex.PW1/16 is de-exhibited). viii. Police complaint dt. 09.01.2020 is Ex.PW1/7. 20. PW1 was cross-examined by the defendant's counsel. During the cross-examination, PW1 stated that she was aware of the facts and contents contained in her evidence affidavit marked as Ex.PW1/A. She stated that she is 70 years old and not formally educated, although she knows a little Urdu. 21. PW1 further deposed that she was employed from 1985 to 2009, working in a garment factory as a supervisor, initially earning a monthly salary of around Rs. 4,000 to Rs. 5,000. She denied the suggestion that her salary was between Rs. 1,000 to Rs. 2,000 per month. She stated that during that period, she was the sole earner in her family, as no one else in her family was working. She sometimes managed to save between Rs. 100 to Rs. 200 per month, and at times even up to Rs. 1,000. By the year 2001, she had saved approximately Rs. 50,000 to Rs. 60,000. 22. PW1 admitted that she was not aware of the exact amount paid for the purchase of the suit property in 2001 and that she did not pay any commission or brokerage to any property dealer. She also could not Civil Suit No.104/20 Judgment dt.09.09.2025 Page no. 7 of 21 recall from whom the property was purchased. She denied the suggestion that her son purchased the property using his own funds. She further stated that construction of the suit property was started by her after 2-3 years, initially constructing the ground floor, followed by a storeroom on the first floor, though she could not recall when the storeroom was constructed. She denied the suggestion that her son constructed the ground floor and the first floor using his own funds. 23. PW1 also stated that her son went to Saudi Arabia around Samima Khatoon vs Mohd. She admitted that she had taken a loan from a neighbor to send her son to Saudi Arabia but did not know the neighbor's name. She deposed that her son got married for the first time in 2009. She alleged that her son and his second wife have been harassing her both physically and mentally, using abusive language and beating her. Initially, she attempted to resolve the disputes by requesting them to live peacefully, but when her requests were ignored, she asked them to leave the house and even to live on rent. When they refused, she formally debarred them from the property. 24. PW1 denied the suggestion that her son dispossessed her from the suit property in 2018. She stated that she voluntarily left the house in 2022 for her safety and began living with her younger daughter, but she still visits the house occasionally. She also denied that the present suit was filed at the instigation of her younger daughter and son-in-law, and further denied that her son and his wife had cared for her properly. Finally, she denied that she was deposing falsely. The cross-examination of PW1 concluded on 04.05.2024. 25. Thereafter, PW2 Sh. Mohd. Aliullah Ansari has tendered his evidentiary affidavit as Ex.PW2/A and relied upon the document i.e. Copy of Aadhar card vide Ex.PW2/1. Civil Suit No.104/20 Judgment dt.09.09.2025 Page no. 8 of 21 26. PW2 was cross-examined by the defendant's counsel. During the cross-examination, PW2 stated that he was aware of the present case and is 47 years old. He stated that he was previously engaged in the garment business and is currently involved in the signboard business. He deposed that he has known both the plaintiff and the defendant for the last 25 years. He mentioned that his house is approximately 100 to 150 meters away from the plaintiff's house at present, but he was unaware of the exact number of houses situated between his residence and the plaintiff's house. 27. PW2 further stated that the mother of the defendant is the owner of the property in dispute. He stated that the plaintiff purchased the property in the year 2001, but he did not know from whom the plaintiff purchased the suit property nor the amount for which it was purchased. He also admitted that he was not present at the time when the plaintiff bought the suit property. He deposed that the plaintiff was working as a supervisor at Chelsia Mills Ltd., Maya Puri, earning around Rs. 2,200 at that time. 28. PW2 denied the suggestion that the suit property was purchased by the defendant using his own funds. He stated that the plaintiff is currently residing with her younger daughter. Finally, he denied the suggestion that he was deposing falsely. The cross- examination of PW2 concluded on 16.10.2024. 29. Thereafter, PW3 Sh. Islam Khan has tendered his evidentiary affidavit vide Ex.PW3/A and relied upon the document i.e. Copy of Aadhar Card vide Ex.PW3/1. 30. PW3 was cross - examined by the defendant's counsel. He further stated that his house is Civil Suit No.104/20 Judgment dt.09.09.2025 Page no. 9 of 21 approximately six to seven houses away from the plaintiff's house. 31. He also admitted that he was not present at the time the plaintiff purchased the suit property. He further stated that he did not know the name of the garment factory where the plaintiff was employed as a supervisor, nor was he aware of the salary the plaintiff was earning at that time. 32. PW3 denied the suggestion that the suit property was purchased by the defendant with his own funds. The cross- examination of PW3 concluded on 16.10.2024. The defendant has examined himself as DW1. In his testimony, DW1 tendered his evidentiary affidavit being Ex.DW1/A and he reiterated the contents of the written statement and also relied upon document i.e. i. Electricity bill is Ex.DW1/1. ii. Electricity bill is Ex.DW1/2. iii. Copy of passport is Ex.DW1/3 (OSR). iv. Copy of election I-card is Ex.DW1/4 (OSR). 34. DW1 was cross - examined by the plaintiff's counsel. During the cross-examination, DW1 stated that he had passed the 10th class in the year 1993 and subsequently completed an ITI course in 1999, attending the classes regularly. He admitted in his evidence affidavit that the property in dispute was purchased by him in his name. However, he Civil Suit No.104/20 Judgment dt.09.09.2025 Page no. 10 of 21 acknowledged that no documents proving his ownership of the suit property were filed in the court records, explaining that the said documents were misplaced while shifting houses. 35. DW1 stated that he purchased the suit property for an amount of Rs. 90,000 in the year 2001, and paid Rs. 10,000 as commission to a middleman, though he could not recall the name of the seller. He denied the suggestion that he had no money to purchase the property as he was studying at that time. He asserted that the suit property was purchased through registered documents. He also stated that he had approached the police station to lodge a complaint regarding the missing ownership documents, but the complaint or NCR could not be traced. 36. DW1 denied the suggestion that he had not purchased the Samima Khatoon vs Mohd. Iqbal Nasir on 9 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/172214367/ 7 suit property in his own name, which is why no ownership documents or police complaint exist. He could not remember whether, in his earlier written statement, he had mentioned that the suit property was purchased in the name of the plaintiff. He confirmed that the plaintiff and his family were living together. He denied the suggestion that he was deposing falsely and also rejected the claim that the suit property was purchased by the plaintiff from her own funds. He acknowledged that his mother worked in a garment factory, specifically doing stitching work, and that, to his knowledge, she worked there until the year 2000. 37. Finally, DW1 denied the suggestion that he has no right, title, or interest in the suit property and that he was residing as a licensee in the suit property merely as the son of the plaintiff (licensor). She had tendered her evidentiary by way of affidavit vide Ex.DW2/1. 39. DW2 was cross-examined by the plaintiff's counsel. Civil Suit No.104/20 Judgment dt.09.09.2025 Page no. 11 of 21 During the cross-examination, DW2 stated that she was only somewhat familiar with the contents of his evidence affidavit, as she did not understand English. She explained that she had narrated the contents in Hindi, which were then translated into English. She further stated that her evidence affidavit was prepared with the assistance of his brother, the defendant. 40. DW2 admitted that she did not know the place where the documents for the purchase of the suit property were executed, as she was at home at the time of the purchase. She stated that the suit property was purchased by the defendant from one Shri Happy in the year 2001 for a sum of Rs. 90,000 to Rs. 95,000. She further acknowledged that she was around 16 years old at the time of the purchase. 41. DW2 confirmed that the plaintiff, who is her mother, used to work in a garment factory. The burden of proof lies upon the Plaintiff to establish that she is entitled to the relief of permanent and mandatory injunction. The Plaintiff claims to be the absolute owner of the suit property comprising the ground and first floors and alleges that she was in prior possession. According to her, the Defendant was permitted to reside in the property as a licensee, along with his wife and children, out of love and affection. Legal notice dated 28.08.2019 (Ex. texts.arguments: She further states that she has no other efficacious remedy except to approach this Hon'ble Court for relief. Hence, the Plaintiff has instituted the present suit seeking following reliefs: i. To pass a decree for Permanent and Mandatory Injunction in favor of the plaintiff and against the defendant, his legal heirs, associates, nominees, agents, assignees, executors, administrators, administrators, servants or administrators, servants or any other person on behalf of the defendant restraining them from selling Civil Suit No.104/20 Judgment dt.09.09.2025 Page no. 3 of 21 alienating, transferring, gifting creating third party interest or not to Per Contra, the Defendant respectfully submits that the present suit filed by the Plaintiff is liable to be dismissed as it is a gross abuse of the process of law, devoid of any cause of action, and has been instituted with malafide intent and in collusion with the plaintiff's daughter and son-in-law, namely Smt. Musarrat Parveen and Sh. Minattulla. 10. The Defendant contends that the plaintiff has fabricated a false and concocted story under their influence in order to dispossess the Defendant and to transfer the property illegally to her daughter. The defendant asserts that he is the true and lawful owner of the suit property, having purchased it in the year 2001 from his own earnings, paid the entire consideration amount in cash, and subsequently constructed the property with his own funds. The plaintiff has no right, title, or interest in the suit property and has failed to produce any documentary evidence or source of funds to support her ownership claim. 11. It is further submitted that the Plaintiff was never in constructive possession of the suit property and has falsely asserted that her belongings continue to remain within the premises. In fact, the Plaintiff herself admitted before the Hon'ble Court on 24.03.2022, during her examination under Order X of the Code of Civil Procedure, that she had been dispossessed by the Defendant in the year 2018 and has since Civil Suit No.104/20 Judgment dt.09.09.2025 Page no. 4 of 21 been residing with her daughter. She further stated that the Defendant and his wife do not permit her to enter the suit property. 12. The Defendant states that the Plaintiff and Defendant were living peacefully together for many years, but due to external influence Samima Khatoon vs Mohd. Iqbal Nasir on 9 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/172214367/ 3 and greed, the Plaintiff has initiated this litigation. The Defendant reserves his right to file an appropriate suit for declaration of ownership and/or injunction against the plaintiff. 13. The Defendant further submits that he is in lawful occupation of the suit property and resides therein with his wife and two children. He has already placed on record valid documentary evidence, including his Voter ID and Passport, which reflect the suit property as his residential address, and which were duly submitted in prior proceedings. 14. All others allegations made by the plaintiff regarding abuse, threats, attempted sale to anti-social elements, and refusal to vacate are specifically denied. The Defendant contends that no legal notice was served upon him, nor has any cause of action arisen in favour of the plaintiff. Furthermore, the Plaintiff has approached the court with unclean hands and has concealed material facts, including her long-term residence with her daughter and lack of possession over the suit property. In view of the above, the Defendant prays that the suit be dismissed with costs, as the plaintiff is not entitled to any relief as claimed. Ld. (2005) 7 SCC 667 and citations i.e. (i) Sant Lal JainVs. Avtar Singh on 12 March 1985 & (ii) Prabirenda Nath Nanday and Anr. vs. Narendra Nath Nanday on 07.02.1957, (iii) Vidya Devi Vs. The State of Himachal Pradesh & Ors on 08.01.2020 of Hon'ble Supreme Court of Samima Khatoon vs Mohd. Iqbal Nasir on 9 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/172214367/ 8 43. Whereas, Ld. Counsel for defendant has also filed final written arguments on record on 19.07.2025 and also has filed copy of judgment titled as Anathula Sudhakar vs. P. Buchi Reddy (Dead) By LRs & Ors on 25.03.2008 of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India, in support of his arguments. 47. Plaintiff further claims that after the Defendant's marriage, both he and his wife began harassing her and threatened to take over the property. Due to fear for her safety, the plaintiff was forced to leave her own house and has been living with her daughter since 25.02.2022. She contends that the license granted to the Defendant was revoked through a public notice dated 12.06.2019 and followed by a legal notice dated 28.08.2019, directing the Defendant to vacate the premises. Despite this, the Defendant continued to occupy the suit property. In response, the Defendant has denied the Plaintiff's ownership and possession of the suit property. He has asserted that he is the true and lawful owner, having purchased the property in the year 2001 for a consideration of 90,000/-, and has thereafter constructed a building thereon from his own resources. The Defendant has further alleged that the present suit is collusive in nature and has been instituted at the behest of the Plaintiff's daughter and son-in-law. 50. It is also contended that during the Plaintiff's statement recorded under Order X of the Code of Civil Procedure on 24.03.2022, she admitted to having been dispossessed from the suit property in the year 2018, which is prior to the filing of the present suit. The Plaintiff also stated that she has since been residing with her younger daughter and has not been permitted by the Defendant to re-enter or reside in the suit Samima Khatoon vs Mohd. Iqbal Nasir on 9 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/172214367/ 9 property. 51. Moving further, in Sudhakar Reddy Vs. Lakshmamma (2014 (4) ALT 647) it was held that "in a suit for perpetual injunction, the key consideration is who is in possession of the suit property as of the date of filing the suit. The court may examine the title of the parties if circumstances so warrant." 54. Similarly, in Balkrishna Dattatreya Galande Vs Balkrishna Rambharose Gupta (2019 Law Suit (SC) 140) The Hon'ble Supreme Court in this case held that "in a suit under Section 38 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, a permanent injunction can only be granted to a person who is in actual possession of the property. The plaintiff must prove actual possession to secure a permanent injunction." 55. Additionally, it is well-established in law, as stated in Maria Margarida Sequeria Fernandes and Ors. vs. Erasmo Jack de Sequeria (Dead) through L. Rs. (21.03.2012 - SC): MANU/SC/0225/2012, that "Possession is important when there are no title documents, but once title documents are presented, the title must be prioritized over possession." Possession cannot be considered in a vacuum. 56. 59. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Suraj Lamp & Industries v. State of Haryana (2012) 1 SCC 656 and Shakeel Ahmed v. Syed Akhlaq Hussain (2023 INSC 1016) has clearly held that "even if these documents i.e. the Agreement to Sell and the Power of Attorney were registered, still it could not be said that the respondent would have acquired title over the property in question. As held in Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy (2008) 4 SCC 594, where the title is in dispute and the Plaintiff is not in possession, a bare suit for injunction is not maintainable. In Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy (2008) 4 SCC 594, the Hon'ble Supreme Court laid down clear guidelines on when a suit for bare injunction is maintainable. It held that " Where the title of the Plaintiff is under a cloud or is disputed, and the Plaintiff is not in possession, he must file a suit for declaration and possession. A suit for bare injunction would not be maintainable in such a case."
